_comment: ElevenLabs Sound Effects settings. Like the voice block, everything here is part
of the SFX cache fingerprint, so changing a value regenerates the assets it
affects and nothing else. No secret belongs in this file.
`model` is deliberately null: an unset model means the provider's own default,
which is better than inventing a model id. The fingerprint records null as a
value, so naming a model later invalidates the assets and nothing before that.
promptMaxCharacters is 400, measured rather than documented. A 476-character
prompt was rejected twice with HTTP 400 -- at 22 seconds and again at 20 -- while
every asset at 385 characters or fewer generated first time, including a
20-second looping bed. So the boundary is somewhere between 386 and 475 and 400 is
a safe ceiling. Validation now catches an over-long prompt for free instead of
spending a call to discover it.
durationLimitsSeconds.max stays at 20 because 20 is proven for a looping bed; 22
has never been shown to work and is not worth a call to find out.
ONE EXCEPTION to the fingerprint line above, and it is deliberate: the `normalize`
block is NOT part of the fingerprint. Its own comment says why -- a level is baked
into the file after generation, so changing the target re-encodes what is already
on disk and never buys the asset again. sfx.fingerprint() names its inputs
explicitly, which is what keeps that true rather than hopeful.
Level baked into the asset FILE after generation, because neither prompting nor
the player can do it. ElevenLabs returns a one-off event at whatever level the
prompt implies but returns a continuous texture -- room tone, channel hiss, a
castor rumble, a stream of keystrokes -- near the noise floor whatever the prompt
says; two rounds of prompt work moved that group about 2 dB. And HTML `volume` is
capped at 1.0, so a cue gain can only ever attenuate.
So the asset is normalised and the cue gain goes back to being a MIX decision.
targetRmsDbfs is where a normalised asset lands: loud enough to sit under speech
at about -22 dBFS without disappearing. peakCeilingDbfs is the harder constraint --
the applied gain is the smaller of what the target asks and what the peak allows,
so a transient-heavy one-shot never clips. Raising is the default and attenuation
is opt-in, so nothing already approved gets quieter by accident.
maxGainDb is a refusal, not a clamp: a file needing more than 40 dB is broken
rather than quiet, and amplifying it 40 dB would deliver 40 dB of hiss.
peakCeilingDbfs IS -3, NOT -1, AND THE RESULT IS CHECKED AGAINST IT. mp3 is lossy:
a decode reconstructs more than the encoder was given. The first real pass aimed
eleven assets at -1.0 and delivered eleven files clamped at 0.0 dBFS, overshooting
by 1.0 to 2.8 dB. So -3 is the headroom the codec needs, and the pass no longer
trusts its own arithmetic: it measures the encoded file and backs the gain off
until the DELIVERED peak is under the ceiling, up to maxCorrections times.
Making the audio smaller without making it worse. Joshua: 'Can we compress audio
or convert to MP3 which is less large?' -- it is already mp3, so the levers are
BITRATE and CHANNELS.
Applies to a sound asset over minBytesToCompress. The original is never lost: it
is kept as <asset>.source.mp3 exactly as normalisation keeps a generated master,
and every pass re-encodes from that rather than from an already-compressed file,
so quality cannot decay run after run.
64 kbps mono for a bed that sits about 36 dB under the narration is inaudible
against the original. The nature bed goes from 18.1 MB to roughly 4.7.
Starting philosophy, not final artistic levels. Voice is the reference and is
never attenuated; everything else is set relative to it and is meant to be
retuned by ear without regenerating a single asset.
A cue's own `gain` wins over `categoryGain`. `duckUnderSpeechTo` is a MULTIPLIER
applied to a sustained bed while a voice clip is playing, so an alarm can be
loud in the gaps and still sit under the dialogue. One-shot foley is not ducked;
it is short enough to read through speech and ducking it would make it mush.
ambience ducks to 0.70 rather than 0.55 after Joshua's first listen: at 0.55 of an
already-quiet bed the room tone was inaudible under speech, which is the opposite
of what a bed is for. It still loses a third of its level while a voice sounds.
Ambience was switched OFF on 2026-09-18 while Joshua had no bed he liked, and back
ON the same day when he supplied one: amb_computer_lab, a real recorded computer
room. Both the browser and the exported mp3 read this switch, so the page and the
file always agree.
To supply more: story-rules/reference/SUPPLYING_AMBIENCE.md. Every supplied file
must carry a credit block -- validation refuses one without it.
Where each kind of sound sits in the finished mix, in dBFS RMS, with the narration
running about -22. scripts/audio.py retune-cues derives every cue gain from these
and the asset's MEASURED level, so a gain survives its asset being regenerated or
renormalised instead of silently becoming wrong.
Set after Joshua listened to the first normalised build and said the sound was
super loud. He was right and the numbers said so: nine cues sat at or above the
narrator's own level, including amb_tombs_array_power_rise -- a bed running under
whole chapters at -21 to -23 dBFS -- and two deep vibrations at -18.8, louder than
the voice. That is what happens when assets are lifted 20 to 27 dB and the gains
that were rescuing them are left in place.
A cue may carry `emphasisDb` in its cue sheet to sit above its category, and the
cue sheet is where such a decision belongs: it is about that moment in the story.
LOWERED 3.1 dB (30% in amplitude) on 2026-09-18: Joshua, on the retuned build, still
found the sound too loud against the voices. Applied to every category so the layer
moves as one and the relationships between cues stay as they were.
LOWERED A FURTHER 6 dB on 2026-09-18, third pass. Joshua, after the 30% cut: SFX
still too loud. Beds now sit about 29 dB under the narration and one-shot events
about 23. If that turns out to be too far, raise these five numbers -- nothing else
needs to change, because every gain is derived from them.
AMBIENCE LOWERED A FURTHER 55% (-6.9 dB) on 2026-09-18 before being switched off,
so that whenever it comes back it starts where Joshua asked rather than where the
last pass left it.
A TONE IS NOT A NOISE, and this table targets RMS as though it were. A 500 Hz sine
at -50 dBFS is plainly audible where a broadband bed at -50 is not, so the sirens
needed roughly 14 dB more attenuation than the table gives -- not because the table
is wrong for beds, but because RMS is a poor predictor for anything tonal. When a
future asset is a tone, expect its emphasisDb to be large and negative.
The DRAMA exports. They were 192 kbps STEREO built from sources that are almost
entirely mono -- paying twice the bitrate for a second channel carrying the same
signal. 96 kbps mono is the same audio at half the size: 36.3 MB becomes about 18.
THE VOICE-ONLY EXPORTS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT TOUCHED. combine joins the clips with
`-c copy`, which is lossless and fast, and re-encoding 500 seconds of narration to
save nine megabytes would spend quality on the one thing the whole project is for.
The silence between clips must also stay at the clips' own format or the copy-join
breaks, which is a good reason not to make that number configurable at all.
Raise these if a stereo mix ever becomes real; nothing else needs to change.
